note: Humayun's Tomb established the Mughal grand garden-tomb typology with its double dome and symmetrical charbagh that directly served as an architectural precursor to the Taj Mahal.
Both monuments were commissioned and embellished in white marble by the Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan, who spent his final captive years at Agra Fort gazing at the Taj Mahal.
Shah Jahan transferred the principal seat of Mughal imperial power from Agra Fort to the Red Fort in Delhi in 1648.
Both Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri were grand architectural projects executed in red sandstone under the direct patronage of Emperor Akbar.
Akbar planned his own mausoleum at Sikandra after having previously founded the imperial city of Fatehpur Sikri.
Jahangir governed from Agra Fort and oversaw the completion of his father Akbar's funerary complex at Sikandra.
The delicate white marble masonry and polychrome floral pietra dura of I'timad-ud-Daulah directly anticipated the masterworks of the Taj Mahal.
Mirza Ghiyas Beg held court as Wazir under Jahangir at Agra Fort, and his daughter Empress Nur Jahan built his mausoleum across the Yamuna.
Shah Jahan commissioned both the Red Fort palace and the Jama Masjid as complementary civic and religious keystones of Shahjahanabad.
Safdarjung's Tomb represents the final iteration of the Mughal enclosed garden-tomb tradition that began with Humayun's Tomb two centuries earlier.
Humayun resided and died at Purana Qila before his widow commissioned his grand garden tomb nearby in Nizamuddin.
Both complexes form a contiguous historic precinct in Mehrauli representing the earliest seat of the Delhi Sultanate.
Tughlaqabad Fort was built as the third historical city of Delhi, moving the sultanate capital eastward from the first city at Qutb/Mehrauli.
Maharaja Jai Singh II built the masonry observatory in Delhi upon the instruction of Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah who resided at the Red Fort.
Humayun's Tomb was the site where Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar surrendered to the British after fleeing the Red Fort in 1857.
The congregational courtyard plan and grand scale of Delhi's Jama Masjid directly reflected the architectural precedent set by the Friday Mosque at Fatehpur Sikri.
Both mausoleums were erected in Agra during Jahangir's reign, marking the stylistic evolution from sandstone to pure white marble.
Safdarjung exercised executive power as prime minister of the Mughal Empire from the court at the Red Fort.
Sikandar Lodi's tomb in Lodhi Gardens introduced the octagonal garden-tomb layout and double-dome technology that directly influenced the design of Humayun's Tomb.
The two garden cemeteries flank opposite sides of Lodhi Road, illustrating the shift from late Sultanate tomb architecture to late Mughal design.
Lodhi Gardens houses the tombs and mosques of the final ruling dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate, which was founded at the Qutb Complex.
The rise of Sher Shah Suri and Humayun at Purana Qila marked the political replacement of the Lodi dynasty interred at Lodhi Gardens.
Purana Qila represents Delhi's sixth historic city, continuing the sequence of capitals begun by Qutb-ud-din Aibak at Qutb Minar.
The four marble minarets rising from the South Gate of Akbar's Tomb at Sikandra directly inspired the four detached minarets of the Taj Mahal.
